newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Flynn appeals to NGOs to lobby on social programmes.
newsitem.headline: Flynn appeals to NGOs to lobby on social programmes.

text.p: Social Affairs Commissioner Padraig Flynn will ask non-governmental organisations (NGOs) on Tuesday to lobby their governments to change the EU treaty to allow social programmes to be adopted by Qualified Majority Vote.

"If that outcome is not secured, the future of programmes and actions of any consequence in the social policy area at European level is in serious danger," Flynn plans to tell the European Parliament social affairs committee.
A text of the speech was made available to Reuters.

Flynn wants to launch a "call to arms" in reaction to a recent European Court of Justice order that blocked the European Commission from spending 12 million Ecus for pilot social projects for the poor and elderly.
The court's president issued the order in response to a bid by Britain, supported by Germany, who argued that the decision to spend the money should have been taken by the Council of Ministers.
It suspended the payment of funds pending a final ruling on the substance of the case.

Flynn says in the text that he will try to convince his colleagues to take a flexible approach to the funds that have been set aside for the programmes in case the court ultimately backs the Commission.
He says he wants the Commission to commit money for projects in 1996 even though the work could not begin before the final judgment.
"That would involve a departure from the normal practice of good budgetary housekeeping which requires that 1996 money be spent on projects which begin in 1996," he says.
"However, my overriding concern is to try to safeguard the possibility of using this money for the purpose for which it was intended..."

The Commission allocated the money after Germany vetoed a programme to help older people and joined with Britain to block the Fourth Programme to combat "social and economic exclusion" in the Social Affairs Council last year.

Germany opposed the programmes because they were based on Article 235 of the EC treaty, which its constitutional court has ruled should be used sparingly. Article 235 allows the EU to act when other treaty provisions do not apply.
It argued that the programmes violated the "subsidiarity" principle, which holds that the EU should step in only when it can act more effectively than national governments.
Britain also voted against the social exclusion programme, saying it was not happy with the results of the Third Programme.

Flynn's text notes that the Commission has proposed to the inter-governmental conference that the treaty be amended to allow such programmes to be adopted by qualified majority, but that it needs the help of NGOs.
"There needs to be intensive lobbying of member state governments to ensure that they are all aware of the strength of feeling on this subject," he says.
However, Britain opposes the idea of amending the treaty to paving the way for more EU action in the area of social programmes, a British official said.

"We would oppose it on the grounds that the only action that is appropriate for the Community level is the exchange of information between member states" on how to tackle problems such as "social exclusion", he said.
The programmes themselves are much better handled at the local level where they can be targeted to the particular problems of those areas, he said.
